sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 68 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: God arises. His enemies are scattered.
study.intro: Thirty-five verses follow God on the march, from Sinai through the wilderness to His chosen mountain in Jerusalem, celebrating Him as the Father of the fatherless who rescues His people and draws the nations to bring Him praise.
study.context: The heading names the choirmaster and calls this a psalm and song of David. Verse 1 quotes the words Moses spoke whenever the ark set out (Numbers 10:35), so the psalm reads like a festival procession of the ark. It moves in stages: God's care for the vulnerable (verses 1–6), His march from Sinai through the wilderness (7–10), victory over kings (11–14), the choice of Zion over the high peaks of Bashan (15–18), praise for daily rescue (19–23), the procession into the sanctuary (24–27) and a call for all kingdoms to sing (28–35). Many Hebrew words here are rare, so translations differ in places. Paul quotes verse 18 in Ephesians 4:8 about Christ's ascension.
study.peopleNote: David is named in the heading. Moses' profile gives background on verse 1, which repeats his words when the ark set out, and on Sinai in verses 8 and 17. Planned paintings show processions, mountains, rain on the wilderness and anonymous worshipers; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: God arises
verses.heading: The ark sets out
verses.meaning: The psalm opens with a battle cry: 'God arises. His enemies are scattered, and those who hate Him flee His presence.' These are nearly the words Moses spoke each time the ark of the covenant set out in the wilderness. The ark stood for God's throne among His people, so lifting it to march meant God Himself was going ahead of them. The verse sets the tone for the whole psalm: when God moves, nothing that opposes Him can stand its ground.
verses.context: Numbers 10:35 records Moses' words when the ark set out: 'Rise up, O LORD! May Your enemies be scattered; may those who hate You flee before You.' Psalm 132:8 also calls God to arise and go to His resting place with the ark.
explore: Arises
To stand up and act. In the Psalms it pictures God moving from waiting to decisive action.
Ark of the covenant
The gold-covered chest holding the covenant tablets, the sign of God's throne among Israel.
verses.reflect: Where do you need to remember that God goes ahead of you rather than behind you?
verses.alt: A procession of priests carries a covered chest on poles along a desert track at dawn.

verses.title: Smoke and wax
verses.heading: Opposition that cannot last
verses.meaning: Two homely pictures describe what happens to the wicked before God. Smoke looks thick and threatening, yet a breeze blows it away. Wax seems solid until it is held near a flame, then it softens and runs. Evil that looks powerful has no lasting strength in the presence of God. The verse does not delight in cruelty; it assures God's people that injustice is temporary and that the One who is holy will not leave it standing forever.
verses.context: Micah 1:4 says the mountains melt beneath the LORD like wax before fire, and Psalm 97:5 says the mountains melt like wax before Him. Hosea 13:3 compares the faithless to smoke escaping through a window.
explore: Smoke
A picture of something that looks impressive but quickly disappears.
Wax
Soft material that melts near heat, used for things that cannot endure God's presence.
verses.reflect: What fear in your life looks solid now but might be like smoke before God?
verses.alt: Wisps of smoke drift away over a hillside while a clay lamp melts a lump of wax beside it.

verses.title: Glad before God
verses.heading: Joy for the righteous
verses.meaning: With the word 'But' the scene turns. The same presence that scatters enemies is a place of gladness for the righteous. They 'rejoice before God' and 'celebrate with joy.' The verse piles up three words for joy, as if one could not hold it all. God's nearness is not something His people need to dread; it is the very source of their celebration. The difference lies not in God changing, but in how people stand toward Him.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 16:11 tells Israel to rejoice before the LORD at the feasts with their families, servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows. Psalm 32:11 calls the righteous to be glad in the LORD and shout for joy.
explore: Righteous
Those in right relationship with God, trusting Him and seeking to live His way.
Before God
In His presence, often meaning at the sanctuary during worship.
verses.reflect: What would it look like to bring real joy, not just duty, into your time with God this week?
verses.alt: Villagers dance with linked arms in a sunlit courtyard during a harvest festival.

verses.title: Rider on the clouds
verses.heading: Sing to His name
verses.meaning: Now the singers call everyone to join: 'Sing to God! Sing praises to His name.' God is called 'Him who rides on the clouds.' Neighboring peoples gave that title to the storm god Baal, so Israel's psalm claims it for the true God alone. He is the one who truly commands weather and sky. His name, the LORD, is given here in a short form, Yah, which also appears in 'Hallelujah,' meaning 'praise the LORD.'
verses.context: Deuteronomy 33:26 says God rides the heavens to help His people and the clouds in His majesty. Isaiah 19:1 shows the LORD riding a swift cloud into Egypt, and Psalm 104:3 says He makes the clouds His chariot.
explore: Yah
A short form of God's covenant name, the LORD, found in 'Hallelujah.'
Rides on the clouds
A royal title showing that God, not any storm idol, rules sky and weather.
verses.reflect: What false sources of security compete for the title that belongs only to God in your life?
verses.alt: Towering white clouds sweep across a wide sky over a valley where people lift their hands in song.

verses.title: Father of the fatherless
verses.heading: God's heart for the vulnerable
verses.meaning: Right after describing God as the mighty cloud rider, the psalm shows where His heart is: He is 'a father of the fatherless and a defender of widows.' In the ancient world, orphans and widows had no one to protect their land or speak for them in court. God takes that role Himself. The One in His 'holy habitation' is not distant from the weakest. His greatness is shown by the care He gives to those others overlook.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 10:18 says God executes justice for the fatherless and the widow. Exodus 22:22–24 warns Israel never to mistreat them, and James 1:27 calls caring for orphans and widows pure religion.
explore: Fatherless
Children without a father to provide, protect and represent them.
Defender
Literally a judge, one who takes up a case and secures justice.
verses.reflect: Who in your community has no one to speak for them, and how might you reflect God's care to them?
verses.alt: A grandmother in a head cloth holds the hand of a small child at a village well.

verses.title: Settled in families
verses.heading: The lonely given a home
verses.meaning: God's care keeps going: He 'settles the lonely in families' and 'leads the prisoners out to prosperity.' The isolated receive a household, and captives walk free into a good future. This recalls Israel's own story, freed from slavery in Egypt and brought toward a land of their own. The last line warns that those who rebel against God choose a 'sun-scorched land,' a picture of the dry, empty life that comes from turning away from Him.
verses.context: Exodus 6:6 promises God will bring Israel out from under the burdens of Egypt. Psalm 107:10–14 describes God freeing prisoners from darkness and chains, and Psalm 113:9 says He settles the barren woman in her home.
explore: Lonely
Literally solitary, someone without family or community around them.
Sun-scorched land
Parched ground, an image of the barrenness of life apart from God.
verses.reflect: Where are you lonely, and where might God be placing you in a family, church or friendship?
verses.alt: A traveler is welcomed through the doorway of a stone house by a family sharing bread.

verses.title: Marching through the wasteland
verses.heading: God leads the way
verses.meaning: The psalm looks back to the wilderness journey. 'When You went out before Your people, when You marched through the wasteland.' God is pictured at the head of the column, like a king leading his troops. Israel did not find its own way across the desert; the pillar of cloud and fire showed the route. 'Selah' pauses the song to let that memory sink in before describing what happened when God came near.
verses.context: Exodus 13:21 says the LORD went ahead of Israel in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night. Judges 5:4 uses almost the same words, 'when You marched from the land of Edom,' in Deborah's song.
explore: Wasteland
Desert or wilderness, the dry land Israel crossed between Egypt and Canaan.
Went out before
Led from the front, as a king or commander goes before an army.
verses.reflect: How has God led you through a dry season in the past, and how does that help you trust Him now?
verses.alt: A long line of families with donkeys crosses a rocky desert beneath a tall column of cloud.

verses.title: The One on Sinai
verses.heading: The earth shook
verses.meaning: When God came to Sinai, 'the earth shook and the heavens poured down rain.' Creation itself reacted to His arrival. Sinai was where God gave the covenant and the law, with thunder, cloud and a trembling mountain. The psalm calls God 'the One on Sinai' and 'the God of Israel,' joining His awesome holiness to His personal commitment to one people. The God who shakes mountains has bound Himself to them by covenant.
verses.context: Exodus 19:16–18 describes thunder, lightning, a thick cloud and the whole mountain trembling as the LORD descended. Judges 5:4–5 also says the earth trembled and the heavens poured rain before the One of Sinai.
explore: Sinai
The mountain where God made His covenant with Israel and gave the law through Moses.
Heavens poured
A storm picture of God's power arriving with rain and thunder.
verses.reflect: What does it mean to you that the God who shook Sinai has also made a personal covenant with His people?
verses.alt: Storm clouds and sheets of rain cover a rugged granite mountain while rocks tumble down its slope.

verses.title: Abundant rain
verses.heading: Refreshing the weary
verses.meaning: After the shaking comes kindness: 'You sent abundant rain, O God; You refreshed Your weary inheritance.' Israel is called God's 'inheritance,' His treasured possession. When they were tired and parched, He sent generous showers. Rain in the land of Canaan was a matter of life and death for crops and flocks, and the Bible often treats it as a direct gift of God's goodness. The same power that frightens is used to restore.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 11:11–14 says the promised land drinks rain from heaven and God gives the early and late rains. Matthew 11:28 records Jesus inviting the weary to come to Him for rest.
explore: Inheritance
God's own people and land, treasured as a family estate.
Weary
Exhausted, faint, like land and people worn down by drought.
verses.reflect: Where are you weary right now, and what kind of refreshment are you asking God to send?
verses.alt: Soft rain falls over green hills and a terraced field where a farmer looks up gratefully.

verses.title: Provided for the poor
verses.heading: Settled in the land
verses.meaning: God's 'flock settled' in the land He refreshed. Israel is pictured as sheep finding pasture after a long trek. The second line narrows the focus: 'from Your bounty You provided for the poor.' God's goodness is not only for the strong or successful; He makes sure the needy are fed. This fits His law, which told farmers to leave the edges of fields for the poor and the foreigner so that the land's plenty would reach everyone.
verses.context: Leviticus 19:9–10 commands leaving the corners of fields and fallen grapes for the poor and the foreigner. Psalm 65:9–11 praises God for watering the land and crowning the year with bounty.
explore: Flock
God's people pictured as sheep living under His watchful care.
Bounty
Goodness and generous provision that overflows to others.
verses.reflect: How could you share some of God's bounty in your life with someone in need this week?
verses.alt: Gleaners gather leftover grain at the edge of a golden field while sheep graze nearby.

verses.title: The command
verses.heading: Women proclaim the news
verses.meaning: Now the scene shifts to victory. 'The Lord gives the command,' a single word from Him decides the battle. Then 'a great company of women proclaim it.' In ancient Israel women often went out singing to announce a victory, as Miriam did after the Red Sea and as women did after David's triumphs. The good news spreads through their voices. God's word goes first, and His people joyfully carry it to everyone.
verses.context: Exodus 15:20–21 shows Miriam and the women with tambourines singing after the Red Sea. 1 Samuel 18:6–7 describes women coming out with singing and dancing after David's victory, and Isaiah 40:9 calls a herald to bring good news.
explore: Command
Literally 'word,' God's spoken decree that brings about what He says.
Proclaim
To announce good news, like a herald bringing word of victory.
verses.reflect: What good news about God's work could you share with someone this week?
verses.alt: A crowd of women with tambourines walks singing down a village road under a bright sky.

verses.title: Dividing the plunder
verses.heading: Kings flee
verses.meaning: The women's song begins: 'Kings and their armies flee in haste.' Proud rulers run away, and the result is almost humorous: 'she who waits at home divides the plunder.' The woman who never went to battle shares in its spoils. It shows that the victory was God's, not the army's. Those who stayed home receive the benefits just as much as those who marched, because the Lord Himself won the day.
verses.context: Judges 5:30 pictures the mother of Sisera expecting plunder that never came, the reverse of this verse. 1 Samuel 30:24 records David's rule that those who stayed with the supplies share equally in the plunder.
explore: Plunder
Goods and treasures taken from a defeated enemy after a battle.
Waits at home
Literally the woman of the house, someone who was not on the battlefield.
verses.reflect: How does knowing a victory belongs to God change the way you think about your own success?
verses.alt: A woman at a village doorway lays out colorful bolts of cloth and bronze bowls to share with neighbors.

verses.title: Silver wings
verses.heading: Treasures among the sheepfolds
verses.meaning: This verse is one of the hardest in the Psalms to translate. The first line, 'Though you lie down among the sheepfolds,' may echo Judges 5:16, where some tribes stayed by their flocks instead of fighting. Even so, the spoils are rich: a dove with wings 'covered with silver' and feathers of 'shimmering gold.' It may describe precious plunder, or Israel herself as God's dove, now glittering with blessing. Either way, God's people end up adorned.
verses.context: Judges 5:16 asks Reuben why it stayed among the sheepfolds listening to the flocks. Psalm 74:19 calls Israel God's dove, and Song of Songs 2:14 uses a dove as a term of endearment.
explore: Sheepfolds
Low stone pens for sheep, or perhaps the saddlebags of pack animals; the word is uncertain.
Dove
A gentle bird often used as a picture of God's beloved people.
verses.reflect: Where has God blessed you beyond what you contributed or deserved?
verses.alt: A dove with sunlit wings that gleam silver and gold rises above low stone sheep pens.

verses.title: Snow on Zalmon
verses.heading: Scattered kings
verses.meaning: When 'the Almighty scattered the kings,' it was 'like the snow falling on Zalmon.' Zalmon was a dark, wooded hill, mentioned near Shechem in Judges 9. Snow falling on it would cover the dark slopes with white flakes. The picture may describe fleeing soldiers scattered like flakes, or bright scattered weapons and bodies, or simply the sudden whiteness of a victory God alone brought. Snow was rare in the region, which made the image striking.
verses.context: Judges 9:48 mentions Mount Zalmon, where Abimelech cut branches. Job 37:6 says God commands the snow to fall on the earth, and Psalm 147:16 says He spreads snow like wool.
explore: Almighty
Hebrew Shaddai, an ancient name for God's overwhelming power.
Zalmon
A dark wooded hill in central Israel; its name may mean 'dark' or 'shady.'
verses.reflect: How might God bring something surprisingly bright to a dark situation you are facing?
verses.alt: Fat snowflakes drift over a dark wooded hillside, whitening the treetops.

verses.title: Mount Bashan
verses.heading: A majestic mountain
verses.meaning: The psalm turns to mountains. 'A mountain of God is Mount Bashan.' The phrase can mean a mighty or towering mountain. Bashan lay east of the Jordan, and its northern edge rises to the snowy peaks of Mount Hermon. The repetition, 'a mountain of many peaks,' admires its rugged height. These mountains were impressive and fertile, famous for oaks and cattle, setting up a contrast with the smaller hill God actually chose.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 3:8–10 describes the land of Bashan east of the Jordan reaching to Mount Hermon. Amos 4:1 mentions the famous cows of Bashan, and Isaiah 2:13 speaks of the oaks of Bashan.
explore: Bashan
A fertile highland east of the Sea of Galilee, near Mount Hermon.
Many peaks
Rugged and humped, a mountain with several summits.
verses.reflect: What impressive things in your life tempt you to think they matter more than they do?
verses.alt: Snow-capped multi-peaked mountains rise over oak forests and pastures with grazing cattle.

verses.title: The chosen mountain
verses.heading: Envy of the peaks
verses.meaning: The high mountains are pictured looking with envy at a smaller hill: 'This is the mountain God chose for His dwelling.' Zion in Jerusalem was far lower than Hermon, but God chose it, and that made it greater. God's choice, not natural grandeur, gives a place its worth. The promise that 'the LORD will surely dwell forever' looks beyond the temple to God's lasting presence with His people.
verses.context: Psalm 132:13–14 says the LORD has chosen Zion as His dwelling and resting place forever. Deuteronomy 12:5 speaks of the place God would choose for His name, and Isaiah 2:2 says His mountain will be raised above the hills.
explore: Gaze in envy
To look with hostile jealousy, like rivals eyeing a favored sibling.
Dwelling
God's chosen place to be present and to meet with His people.
verses.reflect: How does knowing that God chooses the small and humble shape the way you see yourself?
verses.alt: A modest hill with a walled city on top glows in evening light while larger dark peaks loom behind.

verses.title: Chariots of God
verses.heading: Sinai in the sanctuary
verses.meaning: God's forces are beyond counting: 'tens of thousands, thousands of thousands.' Earthly kings boasted of their chariots, but God's heavenly army dwarfs them all. The second line makes a bold claim: 'the Lord is in His sanctuary as He was at Sinai.' The same holy presence that came down on the mountain in thunder now rests in Jerusalem's sanctuary. Sinai has, in a sense, moved to Zion. God's glory is present in the place of worship.
verses.context: 2 Kings 6:17 tells of Elisha's servant seeing hills full of horses and chariots of fire. Deuteronomy 33:2 says the LORD came from Sinai with myriads of holy ones, and Daniel 7:10 sees thousands upon thousands serving God.
explore: Chariots
War vehicles, here picturing the countless angelic hosts at God's command.
Sanctuary
The holy place of worship, God's dwelling among His people.
verses.reflect: How might it change your worries to remember that God's unseen resources are beyond counting?
verses.alt: Countless shining lights stream like a vast column across a starlit sky above a hilltop city.

verses.title: Ascended on high
verses.heading: The conqueror receives gifts
verses.meaning: God is pictured as a victorious king climbing to His throne on Zion, leading captives behind Him and receiving gifts, even from those who had rebelled. It celebrates that God has won and taken up residence among His people. In Ephesians 4:8, Paul quotes this verse about Christ: after His victory He ascended and gave gifts to His people. Paul reads the psalm in light of Jesus, the King who conquers and then shares the spoils.
verses.context: Ephesians 4:7–11 quotes this verse, saying Christ ascended on high, led captives and gave gifts to men, such as apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers. Colossians 2:15 says Christ triumphed over powers and authorities.
explore: Ascended
Went up, here pictured as climbing to a throne on God's holy mountain.
Led captives
A victory parade image in which defeated enemies follow the conqueror.
verses.reflect: What gift has the risen Christ given you to use in serving others?
verses.alt: A procession winds up a hill road toward city gates while people carry baskets of gifts.

verses.title: Bears our burden
verses.heading: Daily care
verses.meaning: After all the battle imagery, this verse turns tender: 'Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears our burden, the God of our salvation.' The Hebrew can also mean that God carries us. The mighty King of armies is the one who shoulders our loads every single day, not just in dramatic moments. Salvation includes ordinary daily help. 'Selah' invites a pause to breathe and give that burden to Him.
verses.context: Isaiah 46:4 says God will carry His people even to old age. 1 Peter 5:7 invites believers to cast all their anxiety on Him because He cares, and Matthew 11:30 says Jesus' yoke is easy and His burden light.
explore: Daily
Day by day, showing God's help is constant, not occasional.
Bears
Carries a load, or carries a person, like a parent holding a child.
verses.reflect: What burden could you hand to God today instead of carrying alone?
verses.alt: A villager sets down a heavy bundle of firewood beside a path as morning sunlight breaks through trees.

verses.title: Rescuer from death
verses.heading: God of deliverance
verses.meaning: Verse 20 states it simply: 'Our God is a God of deliverance; the Lord GOD is our rescuer from death.' Literally, 'to the Lord belong the ways out from death.' Death is the final enemy no human can defeat, but God holds the exits. For Israel this meant rescue from enemies and danger. For Christians it points forward to the resurrection, where Jesus breaks death's hold for everyone who trusts Him.
verses.context: Psalm 49:15 says God will redeem the soul from the power of Sheol. Hosea 13:14 promises ransom from the grave, and 1 Corinthians 15:55–57 celebrates victory over death through Christ.
explore: Deliverance
Rescue and salvation, bringing someone safely out of danger.
Ways out
The Hebrew pictures escape routes from death that God alone controls.
verses.reflect: How does God's power over death give you courage for what you fear most?
verses.alt: Light pours through the open entrance of a rock-cut tomb onto a garden path.

verses.title: Crushed heads
verses.heading: Judgment on the defiant
verses.meaning: The language becomes fierce. God 'will crush the heads of His enemies, the hairy crowns of those who persist in guilty ways.' The 'hairy crown' may refer to warriors who let their hair grow as a vow or sign of defiance. The key phrase is 'persist in guilty ways'; this is judgment on those who stubbornly continue in evil. It echoes the promise in Genesis 3:15 that the serpent's head would be crushed, a promise fulfilled by Christ.
verses.context: Genesis 3:15 promises the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head. Psalm 110:6 says the King will crush leaders over the earth, and Romans 16:20 says God will soon crush Satan under your feet.
explore: Hairy crown
The long-haired head of a proud warrior, a sign of defiance.
Persist
Keep walking in a way, here refusing to turn from guilt.
verses.reflect: Is there a pattern of wrong you have been persisting in that God is calling you to leave?
verses.alt: A broken bronze helmet lies on a rocky path beneath a calm sky.

verses.title: From Bashan and the sea
verses.heading: No hiding place
verses.meaning: God speaks: 'I will retrieve them from Bashan, I will bring them up from the depths of the sea.' Bashan's high mountains and the sea's depths are the two extremes of the known world. Whether enemies flee to the heights or the depths, they cannot escape Him. The same idea comforts God's people elsewhere: no matter where they are scattered, God can bring them home. His reach has no limits.
verses.context: Amos 9:2–3 says that even if the wicked dig into Sheol, climb to heaven or hide on Carmel or the sea floor, God will find them. Psalm 139:7–10 says there is nowhere to flee from God's presence.
explore: Bashan
The northern highlands, here picturing the heights.
Depths of the sea
The deepest places, here picturing the farthest hiding place.
verses.reflect: Where might you be trying to hide from God, and what would it mean to let Him find you?
verses.alt: Mountain peaks on one side and a deep blue sea on the other frame a wide valley at sunrise.

verses.title: Complete victory
verses.heading: A grim battlefield picture
verses.meaning: This verse completes God's words with a stark battlefield picture: the foes are so thoroughly defeated that their blood lies on the ground. Ancient victory songs often used shocking images to show that a threat was entirely ended. The point is not to enjoy suffering but to declare that God's justice is final and the enemies who threatened His people will never rise again. Readers can mourn violence while trusting that God will end all evil.
verses.context: 1 Kings 21:19 and 22:38 describe dogs licking Ahab's blood as judgment. Isaiah 63:1–6 pictures God returning from judging with stained garments, and Revelation 19:11–16 shows Christ as the faithful warrior who judges in righteousness.
explore: Foes
Enemies who stubbornly oppose God and threaten His people.
Victory song language
Vivid images used in ancient poetry to show total defeat of a threat.
verses.reflect: How can you trust God's justice in situations where evil seems to win?
verses.alt: An empty battlefield at dusk with abandoned shields and a fading red sky, with no people visible.

verses.title: The procession
verses.heading: God enters the sanctuary
verses.meaning: Now the psalm describes worship itself: 'They have seen Your procession, O God, the march of my God and King into the sanctuary.' The victorious march that began at Sinai ends at the temple. People watch the parade, likely with the ark, as Israel's true King enters His house. The words 'my God and King' are personal; the singer is not just reporting history but declaring loyalty to this King.
verses.context: 2 Samuel 6:12–15 tells how David brought the ark into Jerusalem with shouting and trumpets. Psalm 24:7–10 calls the gates to lift up so the King of glory may come in.
explore: Procession
A solemn, joyful parade in worship, here likely with the ark.
Sanctuary
The holy place where God's presence dwelt among Israel.
verses.reflect: In what ways can you welcome God as King into the everyday 'house' of your life?
verses.alt: Crowds line a stone street as a festive procession with banners climbs toward a hilltop sanctuary.

verses.title: Singers and tambourines
verses.heading: The order of worship
verses.meaning: The verse gives a glimpse of the parade: 'The singers lead the way, the musicians follow after, among the maidens playing tambourines.' Voices, instruments and dancing women all have a place. Worship in Israel was full, joyful and organized. Each group had a role, and together they made a single celebration. It shows that praising God involves the whole person and the whole community, young and old, men and women.
verses.context: 1 Chronicles 15:16 shows David appointing Levite singers with harps, lyres and cymbals. Exodus 15:20 tells of Miriam leading women with tambourines, and Psalm 150:4 calls for praise with tambourine and dancing.
explore: Musicians
Players of harps and other stringed instruments in the procession.
Tambourines
Small hand drums often played by women at celebrations and victories.
verses.reflect: What part could you play in helping your community worship together?
verses.alt: Young women with tambourines dance behind a group of singers along a sunny path.

verses.title: Bless in the congregation
verses.heading: From the fountain of Israel
verses.meaning: The worshipers call out: 'Bless God in the great congregation; bless the LORD from the fountain of Israel.' 'Fountain of Israel' likely means all those who flow from Israel's family line, the descendants of Jacob, the source of the nation. Praise is not private here but public, offered together by the whole assembly. To 'bless' God means to speak well of Him, thanking and honoring Him for all He has done.
verses.context: Psalm 22:22 promises to praise God in the midst of the assembly. Psalm 26:12 says 'in the congregations I will bless the LORD,' and Isaiah 48:1 speaks of those who came from the waters of Judah.
explore: Congregation
The assembled people of God gathered together for public worship.
Fountain
A spring or source, here the ancestral source of Israel's people.
verses.reflect: Why does it matter to praise God together with others and not only alone?
verses.alt: A large crowd gathers in an open stone courtyard beside a flowing spring, raising hands together.

verses.title: The tribes in procession
verses.heading: Benjamin and the princes
verses.meaning: The tribes are named as they march: little Benjamin first, then the princes of Judah, Zebulun and Naphtali. Benjamin was the youngest son of Jacob and among the smallest tribes, yet it leads the way; it gave Israel its first king, Saul. Judah was in the south; Zebulun and Naphtali were in the far north. Together they show the whole nation, south and north, large and small, united in worshiping God.
verses.context: Judges 5:18 praises Zebulun and Naphtali for risking their lives in battle. 1 Samuel 9:21 shows Saul calling Benjamin the smallest tribe, and Isaiah 9:1 promises honor to the land of Zebulun and Naphtali.
explore: Benjamin
The youngest son of Jacob and a small tribe that produced King Saul.
Princes
Tribal leaders and officials marching in the parade.
verses.reflect: How does God use the small and overlooked to lead the way in your community?
verses.alt: Groups of people under different colored banners walk together up a winding road toward the city.

verses.title: Summon Your power
verses.heading: Do it again
verses.meaning: The psalm turns to prayer: 'Summon Your power, O God; show Your strength, O God, which You have exerted on our behalf.' Having remembered all God did in the past, the people ask Him to act again. Past faithfulness becomes the basis for present requests. The phrase 'on our behalf' reminds them that God's mighty acts were not random displays of power but were done for His people's good.
verses.context: Isaiah 51:9 cries, 'Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD, as in days of old.' Habakkuk 3:2 prays, 'Revive Your work in these years,' and Psalm 44:1–4 recalls past victories before asking for help.
explore: Summon
To command or call up, asking God to display His strength.
Exerted
Worked or accomplished, showing God's power in action for His people.
verses.reflect: What has God done for you in the past that you can bring to Him as a reason to ask for help now?
verses.alt: A man kneels on a hillside at dawn with an open scroll beside him, looking toward the rising sun.

verses.title: Gifts to the temple
verses.heading: Kings bring tribute
verses.meaning: 'Because of Your temple at Jerusalem kings will bring You gifts.' The temple stands for God's presence, and that presence draws even foreign rulers to come with tribute. In Solomon's day, the Queen of Sheba and other monarchs came bearing gifts. The verse looks beyond that to a day when nations would honor the true God. The wise men bringing gifts to the child Jesus are an early fulfillment of that hope.
verses.context: 1 Kings 10:23–25 tells of kings seeking Solomon and bringing gifts. Isaiah 60:5–6 says the wealth of nations will come to Zion, and Matthew 2:11 shows the wise men offering gold, frankincense and myrrh.
explore: Temple
God's house in Jerusalem, the place where His presence dwelt.
Gifts
Tribute brought in honor, a sign of recognizing someone's greatness.
verses.reflect: What gift of time, talent or resources could you bring to God this week?
verses.alt: Foreign envoys with camels carry chests and jars up a road toward a walled city on a hill.

verses.title: The beast in the reeds
verses.heading: Rebuke the warlike
verses.meaning: 'Rebuke the beast in the reeds' likely refers to Egypt, pictured as a crocodile or hippopotamus lurking in the Nile's papyrus marshes. The 'herd of bulls among the calves' may describe powerful nations and their lesser allies. The prayer asks God to humble them until they submit, 'bringing bars of silver' as tribute. The final line, 'Scatter the nations who delight in war,' shows God's goal is not violence but peace.
verses.context: Ezekiel 29:3 calls Pharaoh a great monster lying in the Nile. Isaiah 2:4 promises nations will beat swords into plowshares, and Psalm 46:9 says God makes wars cease to the ends of the earth.
explore: Beast in the reeds
A river creature, likely a symbol for Egypt and its power.
Delight in war
Love violence and conquest, the opposite of God's purpose of peace.
verses.reflect: Where do you see a love of conflict in the world, or in yourself, that needs God's rebuke?
verses.alt: Tall papyrus reeds line a broad river where a crocodile rests half-hidden in the water.

verses.title: Egypt and Cush
verses.heading: Hands stretched to God
verses.meaning: Two distant powers turn toward God: 'Envoys will arrive from Egypt; Cush will stretch out her hands to God.' Egypt was Israel's ancient oppressor, and Cush lay far to the south along the upper Nile. Even former enemies and faraway peoples will come in worship. Stretching out hands was a posture of prayer. This hope is fulfilled in Acts 8, where an Ethiopian official believes in Jesus and is baptized.
verses.context: Isaiah 19:21–25 promises Egypt will know the LORD and worship Him. Zephaniah 3:10 says worshipers will come from beyond the rivers of Cush, and Acts 8:27–38 tells of the Ethiopian official's baptism.
explore: Envoys
Official messengers or ambassadors sent by a nation.
Cush
The land south of Egypt, roughly ancient Nubia in today's Sudan.
verses.reflect: How does God's welcome for faraway peoples shape how you treat people from other backgrounds?
verses.alt: A traveler in a chariot reads a scroll on a desert road as a companion walks alongside.

verses.title: Kingdoms of the earth
verses.heading: Everyone sing
verses.meaning: The call widens to the whole world: 'Sing to God, O kingdoms of the earth; sing praises to the Lord.' The psalm began with Israel's procession, but it ends inviting every nation to join the song. God is not a tribal deity; He is Lord of all. 'Selah' pauses the music, as if waiting for the nations to respond. It anticipates the scene in Revelation, where people from every tribe and language worship God together.
verses.context: Psalm 67:3–4 calls all peoples to praise God. Psalm 117:1 says, 'Praise the LORD, all you nations,' and Revelation 7:9–10 shows a multitude from every nation praising God.
explore: Kingdoms
Nations and their rulers, the political powers of the world.
Sing praises
To make music in honor of God, often with instruments.
verses.reflect: How can you join in the worldwide song of praise to God?
verses.alt: People in many styles of dress stand together on a hillside, singing as the sun rises.

verses.title: Highest heavens
verses.heading: His mighty voice
verses.meaning: The nations sing 'to Him who rides upon the highest heavens of old.' This picks up the cloud-rider image of verse 4 and expands it; God rules the oldest and highest heavens, existing before all things. Then: 'behold, His mighty voice resounds.' God's voice, often heard in thunder, is powerful and effective. When He speaks, things happen. The universe itself echoes with His authority.
verses.context: Psalm 29:3–9 describes the voice of the LORD thundering over the waters and shaking the wilderness. Deuteronomy 33:26 says God rides the heavens, and Hebrews 1:3 says He upholds all things by His powerful word.
explore: Highest heavens
Literally 'heavens of heavens,' the farthest reaches of the sky.
Voice
God's spoken word, often pictured in the Psalms as rolling thunder.
verses.reflect: What do you hear God saying to you through His Word today?
verses.alt: Lightning flashes over vast starry heavens above a quiet sleeping village.

verses.title: Ascribe the power
verses.heading: Majesty over Israel
verses.meaning: 'Ascribe the power to God' means to recognize and openly declare that all strength belongs to Him. His 'majesty is over Israel,' showing His special care for His people, and 'His strength is in the skies,' showing His rule over all creation. These two lines hold together God's closeness and His greatness. He is the God of one people and the Lord of the entire cosmos at the same time.
verses.context: Psalm 29:1–2 calls the heavenly beings to ascribe glory and strength to the LORD. Deuteronomy 33:26 says He rides the skies in His majesty, and 1 Chronicles 29:11 says the power and glory belong to Him.
explore: Ascribe
To give credit, to declare that something belongs to someone.
Majesty
Splendor and exalted dignity, the royal greatness that belongs to God.
verses.reflect: Where are you tempted to take credit for strength that really comes from God?
verses.alt: A wide blue sky with towering clouds stretches over a peaceful countryside of fields and villages.

verses.title: Awesome in His sanctuary
verses.heading: Strength given to His people
verses.meaning: The psalm ends with wonder: 'O God, You are awesome in Your sanctuary.' The God who marched from Sinai now dwells among His people, and His presence inspires reverent awe. But He does not keep His strength to Himself; He 'gives strength and power to His people.' His might becomes their help. The last words, 'Blessed be God!' sum up the whole song with a single shout of praise.
verses.context: Isaiah 40:29–31 promises that God gives power to the weak and those who wait on Him renew their strength. Ephesians 3:16 prays for strength through God's Spirit, and Psalm 29:11 says the LORD gives strength to His people.
explore: Awesome
Inspiring holy fear and wonder, so great that people tremble with reverence.
Gives strength
God shares His power to help His people live, serve and endure.
verses.reflect: Where do you need God to give you strength today, and how can you ask Him for it?
verses.alt: People leave a hilltop sanctuary at sunset, walking down the path with confident steps.
